claims.text: Severe plastic deformation followed by controlled annealing can create a heterogeneous gradient microstructure.
A heterogeneous gradient microstructure can concurrently improve strength and ductility in metals.
The proposed gradient microstructure contains alternating soft and hard regions.
The deformation and annealing process can be tuned to induce a gradient heterostructure.
Clear soft and hard domains must be established without excessive grain growth to obtain the proposed improvement.
Maintaining optimal phase boundaries is necessary for the proposed improvement.
The gradient heterostructure contains fine, strong-grained regions and coarse, ductile-grained regions.
Fine- and coarse-grained regions promote strain partitioning.
The heterostructured microstructure triggers strain partitioning.
The heterostructured microstructure promotes the formation of geometrically necessary dislocations.
Strain partitioning and geometrically necessary dislocations balance load between high-strength and high-ductility regions.
Load balancing between heterogeneous regions delays localized necking and failure.
The proposed processing route will increase tensile strength relative to a conventionally processed homogeneous control.
The proposed processing route will increase ductility relative to a conventionally processed homogeneous control.
Improvement may be limited or reversed when deformation intensity or annealing conditions are not optimized.
Over-annealing may limit or reverse the concurrent strength–ductility improvement.
Excessive dislocation density may limit or reverse the concurrent strength–ductility improvement.
The magnitude of strength and ductility enhancement depends on processing conditions and metal composition.
